- If sentiment is positive (≥0.20) and forecast is rising steadily, reduce forecast slope to avoid over-optimism.  
- If sentiment is negative (≤0.00) and forecast is rising, cap upward momentum; price may not sustain rally.  
- If recent history shows sharp upward moves (e.g., >75% spike in 3–5 days), model tends to over-forecast; apply downward bias to next 5–7 days.  
- If forecast is flat or slightly rising but true outcome shows strong upward trend, model underestimates momentum — increase forecast by 2–5% for next 3–5 days.  
- If forecast is rising sharply after a dip, check for sentiment lag — if sentiment is neutral or negative, reduce forecast peak to avoid overshoot.  
- If true outcome shows mean reversion after a spike, model often fails to correct — apply downward bias to forecast 3–5 days after peak.  
- If sentiment is positive but forecast is flat or declining, model underreacts — increase forecast slightly to align with sentiment.  
- For 30-day horizon, if forecast is consistently above true outcome by >5% for 3+ consecutive days, reduce forecast by 1–2% per day to avoid overestimation.  
- If sentiment is positive and true outcome is volatile, model tends to smooth out — increase forecast volatility slightly to reflect sentiment-driven uncertainty.
